Why the TFSA limit is stuck at $7,000, and when it moves: inflation indexing in $500 steps

Rebuild the TFSA dollar limit from the law: $5,000 indexed to CPI each year since 2009 and rounded to the nearest $500. See why the limit stays flat for years and then jumps, what 18 years of room is worth in today’s prices, and when the next steps arrive under different inflation rates.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 26 October 2026 · 8 min read
Sources reviewed 26 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Follow the TFSA dollar limit as it is indexed to inflation in CAD 500 steps

Limits for 2009 to 2026 are CRA’s published figures. Since 2016 the law sets the limit at $5,000 indexed for each year after 2009 by the section 117.1 CPI factor and rounded to the nearest $500 (a tie rounds up). The 2027 factor of 2.6% is this page’s calculation from Statistics Canada CPI to September 2026; CRA had not published the 2027 limit when it was checked on 26 October 2026. From 2028 the chart applies the 2% inflation you enter every year (rounded to 0.1 percentage point, as the factor is), which is an assumption, not a forecast, and Parliament can change the limit. Room is counted from the year you turned 18, assuming Canadian residence in every year since. Contribution room also depends on your own history: unused room carries forward, withdrawals are added back the following year, and over-contributions are taxed.

The central idea

The TFSA dollar limit is $5,000 indexed to inflation since 2009, rounded to the nearest $500. That keeps new room roughly constant in real terms: the $109,000 of limits from 2009 to 2026 is worth about $138,600 in September 2026 prices. A flat limit is not a cut, and a jump is not a gift; both are rounding. Indexing protects the size of the room, not the value of what you hold in it.

01

Three years at $7,000 is not a freeze

The TFSA dollar limit was $7,000 in 2024, 2025 and 2026. Prices rose in each of those years, so it is natural to ask whether the room is quietly shrinking, or whether the government has stopped indexing it. Neither is the case. The limit is still tied to inflation; it simply moves in steps of $500, and inflation of about 2% a year takes several years to add up to a step.

This guide rebuilds the limit from the law, year by year, using the same consumer price index the law uses. It then answers four practical questions: why the limit sits still and then jumps, how much the room has really been worth, what the 2027 figure is likely to be, and how quickly future steps come under different inflation rates. The tool below lets you change your age, which sets your first eligible year, the inflation you assume after 2027 and how far ahead to look.

One distinction runs through the whole page. The TFSA is an account with tax rules; it is not an investment. The limit decides how much you may put in. What happens to that money depends on what you buy inside the account, which can be a savings deposit, a GIC, a balanced fund or an equity fund, each with its own risk, fees and liquidity.

02

The rule: $5,000, indexed since 2009, rounded to the nearest $500

Section 207.01 of the Income Tax Act defines the “TFSA dollar limit”. For 2009 to 2012 it was $5,000; for 2013 and 2014, $5,500; for 2015, $10,000. For every year after 2015 it is “$5,000 adjusted for each year after 2009” under section 117.1, rounded to the nearest multiple of $500, with an exact tie rounded up. CRA’s indexation page describes the same rule: the limit is fixed at $5,000, indexed for each year after 2009 and rounded to the nearest $500.

Section 117.1 sets the yearly factor. It divides the average CPI for the 12 months ending on 30 September before the year by the average for the 12 months before that, subtracts one, and rounds to the nearest 0.1%. The same factors index the federal tax brackets and many credits, which is why the TFSA step and the bracket increase are announced together each autumn.

Two features matter. First, the unrounded amount keeps compounding every year, whether or not the published limit moves. Second, the 2013–2014 and 2015 limits were written directly into the law, so they sit above or off the indexed path. Since 2016 every limit has been the rounded indexed amount.

03

Chart 1: a smooth indexed amount, a stepped limit

The first chart shows both lines. The dashed line is $5,000 compounded by each year’s factor. The solid line is the limit you actually receive. Recomputing the factors from Statistics Canada CPI gives 0.6% for 2010, 2.8% for 2012, 1.0% for 2021, then 6.3%, 4.7%, 2.7% and 2.0% for 2023 to 2026; the last four are exactly the rates CRA lists, and the rounded results reproduce every published limit from 2016 to 2026.

By 2026 the unrounded amount is about $7,184.92. That is closer to $7,000 than to $7,500, so the limit stayed at $7,000. Unless inflation is very low, a few more years of growth push it past $7,250 and the limit steps up. The large 2023 factor (6.3%) explains the quick move from $6,000 in 2022 to $6,500 in 2023 and $7,000 in 2024: high inflation brought the steps closer together.

Change the inflation assumption and the projected steps move. At 2% a year after 2027, the projected limit is $8,000 by 2030, $8,500 by 2033 and $9,500 by 2039. At 1% the next steps arrive years later. These projections only apply the rule; they do not predict prices, and Parliament can change the rule itself, as it did in 2015 and 2016.

04

Chart 2: rounding gives and takes, but never accumulates

The second chart shows how far each year’s limit is from the unrounded amount. In 2018 the limit of $5,500 was about $222 below the indexed $5,721.70; in 2019 the limit of $6,000 was about $152 above $5,847.57. In 2026 the limit is about $185 below.

Because the law compounds the unrounded amount, not the rounded limit, these gaps do not build up. A year when rounding gives less room is not carried forward as a deficit, and a generous year is not taken back. Over many years the published limits track the indexed amount closely; the bars bounce within $250 either side of zero.

For a saver, the lesson is not to read policy into a single year’s figure. A flat limit after a year of inflation means the unrounded amount has not yet crossed the next halfway mark. A $500 jump after a mild year usually means it just did.

05

Chart 3: what each year’s room is worth in today’s prices

The third chart converts each year’s limit into September 2026 prices using the all-items CPI (Statistics Canada table 18-10-0004-01), dividing CPI for September 2026 (170.0) by CPI for January of the year the room arrived. The 2009 limit of $5,000 is worth about $7,522 in those prices. The 2026 limit of $7,000 is worth about $7,212, because prices rose between January and September 2026.

Most years land between about $7,000 and $7,750 in today’s prices. The outlier is 2015, whose $10,000 limit is worth about $13,677. Indexing has done what it was designed to do: each year’s new room buys roughly the same amount of goods and services.

Added up, the $109,000 of limits from 2009 to 2026 is worth about $138,617 in September 2026 prices. If you turned 18 after 2009, enter your age; someone aged 29 at the end of 2026, first eligible in 2015, has $78,000 of limits worth about $94,148. These totals describe room, not wealth. Room only becomes wealth when money is contributed and invested, and they apply only to someone who has been 18 or older and resident in Canada in every year counted.

06

What the September 2026 CPI implies for 2027

Statistics Canada’s CPI for September 2026 completes the averaging window for the 2027 factor. The average CPI for October 2025 to September 2026 is 167.525, against 163.275 for October 2024 to September 2025. The ratio gives a factor of 2.6% after rounding. Applied to the unrounded 2026 amount, it gives about $7,371.72, which rounds to $7,500.

Treat this as a calculation, not an announcement. When this page was checked on 26 October 2026, CRA’s limits page listed TFSA limits only to 2026 and CRA’s indexation page showed factors only to 2026. Section 117.1 also allows the CPI to be “adjusted in such manner as may be prescribed”. The margin here is wide: the unrounded amount would need to fall below $7,250 to keep the limit at $7,000, which would take a factor of 0.9% or less. Even so, contribute based on CRA’s published figure and your own room in My Account, not on this projection.

A higher limit adds room on 1 January. It does not change room you already have, does not raise the limit on past years, and does not make any investment inside the account safer or more rewarding.

07

Chart 4: how long the next steps take

The heatmap asks how many years after 2026 the limit first reaches $7,500, $8,000, $8,500, $9,000 and $10,000, for constant inflation rates from 0.5% to 4% after 2027. Every row starts from the calculated $7,500 for 2027, so the first column is one year throughout.

At 2% a year, the limit reaches $8,000 in four years, $9,000 in ten and $10,000 in sixteen. At 1% a year it takes seven years to reach $8,000 and thirty to reach $10,000. At 3% it reaches $10,000 in eleven. Each $500 step needs the unrounded amount to grow by about $500, which is around 7% of the current limit, so at 2% inflation a step arrives roughly every three to four years.

Inflation does not arrive at a constant rate, so the real calendar will be lumpier than any single row. The rows are useful for planning a contribution budget: if you plan to fill your room each year from pay, expect the required amount to rise in occasional $500 jumps rather than every year.

08

Using the limit sensibly inside a long-term plan

  1. Know your own room. The yearly limit is only one part. Unused room carries forward; amounts withdrawn are added back on 1 January of the following year; and over-contributions are taxed at 1% a month. The TFSA recontribution calendar follows those rules. Losses inside the account do not restore room; the loss and room guide shows why.
  2. Keep the account and the investment separate. Income and gains earned inside a TFSA are generally not taxed and withdrawals are not taxable, but those are account rules. A balanced fund held in a TFSA is still exposed to market falls, fund fees and uncertain returns. The asset location guide compares what to hold where.
  3. Distinguish new pay from an existing lump sum. Saving from each paycheque grows with income and the limit rises occasionally; moving an existing non-registered holding into a TFSA is a different decision, because transferring units in kind is a disposition at market value. The in-kind contribution guide covers it.
  4. Index your own contributions, not just the room. If your plan is to save a fixed share of income, the inflation-adjusted contribution guide shows why a flat dollar amount loses ground over decades. The RRSP and TFSA comparison covers which account to fill first.

Sources and scope

Public sources reviewed on 26 October 2026. Limits for 2009 to 2026 are CRA’s published figures. Indexation factors are recomputed from Statistics Canada’s all-items CPI under section 117.1 of the Income Tax Act and match every factor CRA lists for 2023 to 2026. The 2027 limit is this page’s calculation from CPI to September 2026, not a CRA announcement. Years from 2028 use an editable inflation assumption, not a forecast. Original scenario calculations and research checklists are TickerLantern’s educational analysis; attributed publisher examples retain their stated source and scope. Recheck current issuer documents for any product-specific decision.

  1. Canada Revenue Agency · MP, DB, RRSP, DPSP, ALDA, TFSA limits, YMPE and the YAMPE ↗

    Reviewed in the in-app browser on 26 October 2026. TFSA dollar limits: $5,000 for 2009–2012, $5,500 for 2013–2014, $10,000 for 2015, $5,500 for 2016–2018, $6,000 for 2019–2022, $6,500 for 2023 and $7,000 for 2024–2026. No 2027 TFSA limit was listed. The $109,000 total is computed on this page.

  2. Canada Revenue Agency · Indexation adjustment for personal income tax and benefit amounts ↗

    Reviewed 26 October 2026: indexation increase of 2.0% for 2026, 2.7% for 2025, 4.7% for 2024 and 6.3% for 2023; annual TFSA dollar limit $7,000 for 2024–2026; footnote stating the limit is fixed at $5,000, indexed for each year after 2009 and rounded to the nearest $500.

  3. Justice Laws · Income Tax Act, section 207.01 (definition of TFSA dollar limit) ↗

    Retrieved 26 October 2026: limits written into the law for 2009–2015, and for each year after 2015 $5,000 adjusted under section 117.1 for each year after 2009, rounded to the nearest $500 with ties rounded up.

  4. Justice Laws · Income Tax Act, section 117.1 (annual adjustment) ↗

    Retrieved 26 October 2026: factor equals the CPI for the 12 months ending 30 September before the year divided by the CPI for the previous 12 months, minus one, adjusted as prescribed and rounded to the nearest one-thousandth.

  5. Statistics Canada · Table 18-10-0004-01, Consumer Price Index, monthly, not seasonally adjusted (all-items, Canada; vector v41690973) ↗

    Monthly all-items CPI (2002=100) retrieved through the Bank of Canada Valet API on 26 October 2026, January 2006 to September 2026 (September 2026 = 170.0). Used to recompute the 2010–2027 indexation factors and to restate each year’s limit in September 2026 prices.

  6. Bank of Canada · Valet API, series V41690973 (Total CPI) ↗

    Republishes the Statistics Canada series above; JSON retrieved 26 October 2026 (SHA-256 recorded in the local release note).
